grades.quote: some process might still hold a reference to the inode in memory
grades.reason: Only touches the layers indirectly. It contrasts the link count (directory entries) with the in-memory reference held by an open process, and notes an inode can be allocated on disk with no directory entry. It never defines the three concepts or compares them directly.

grades.quote: The file’s inode and the disk space holding its content are only freed when the file’s link count is zero and no file descriptors refer to it.
grades.reason: Directly separates the layers. A directory entry (link) is a name plus a reference to an inode. The inode holds the metadata, link count and content location. A file descriptor refers to an inode, as shown by fstat. The file is freed only when the link count is zero and no file descriptors refer to it.

grades.quote: Each inode provides the metadata for one file.
grades.reason: Explains the inode layer well: it holds one file's metadata and block mapping, and is identified by its inode number. It only hints that directories map names to inode numbers, and it says nothing about file descriptors. That makes it a useful part of the answer.

grades.quote: The operating system removes the file when it no longer has any names and is no longer in use by any process.
grades.reason: Explains the directory-entry layer: names are links to a file and its metadata, and link/unlink add or remove names. It also separates names from the file's existence, since the file persists while a process is using it. It never names inodes or file descriptors explicitly, so it covers only part of the question.
